questions.enonce_markdown: What do you understand by tissue respiration? *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown: **Tissue (cellular or internal) respiration** is the **series of enzyme-controlled reactions in the living cells of the tissues by which organic food molecules (mainly glucose) are oxidised, step by step, to release energy**, which is used to make **ATP**. In aerobic conditions the end products are carbon dioxide and water (the glucose equation is $C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \to 6CO_2 + 6H_2O + \text{energy}$); in anaerobic conditions, lactate or ethanol and CO$_2$. It occurs in the **cytoplasm and mitochondria** of every living cell, and is distinct from gaseous exchange (breathing), which supplies the oxygen.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) What are the major phases of tissue respiration.

(ii) Where do these major phases occur?

(iii) What are the respective products of each of the major phases of tissue respiration?

(iv) What is the net ATP produced in each phase of tissue respiration? *[12 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
| Phase | (ii) Where it occurs | (iii) Products | (iv) Net ATP per glucose |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Glycolysis** (breakdown of glucose to pyruvate) | **Cytoplasm (cytosol)** | 2 pyruvate (3C), 2 reduced NAD (NADH + H$^+$) | **2 ATP** (4 made, 2 used to start the process) by substrate-level phosphorylation |
| **Link reaction** (oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate; the link between phases 1 and 2) | **Matrix of the mitochondrion** | 2 acetyl-coenzyme A (2C), 2 CO$_2$, 2 NADH | none directly |
| **2. Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle)** | **Matrix of the mitochondrion** | for the two turns per glucose: 4 CO$_2$, 6 NADH, 2 FADH$_2$ (reduced FAD), 2 ATP | **2 ATP** (substrate-level phosphorylation) |
| **3. Electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation** | **Inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae)** | **ATP** and **water** (oxygen is the final electron acceptor); NAD and FAD are regenerated | about **34 ATP** (classical value); modern value about 26 to 28 |

**(i) Major phases.** Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle (preceded by the link reaction) and the electron transport chain with oxidative phosphorylation (the three major phases).

**Explanations.**

- *Glycolysis:* glucose (6C) is phosphorylated using 2 ATP, split into two triose phosphates and oxidised to two pyruvate; 4 ATP and 2 NADH are formed. No oxygen is needed.
- *Link reaction and Krebs cycle:* in the presence of oxygen pyruvate enters the mitochondrion, loses CO$_2$ and hydrogen to form acetyl CoA; this joins oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C), which is oxidised back to oxaloacetate, releasing CO$_2$ and hydrogen carried by NAD and FAD.
- *Electron transport chain:* the hydrogen carried by NADH and FADH$_2$ gives up electrons to carriers in the cristae; the energy released pumps protons into the intermembrane space, and the protons flow back through **ATP synthase**, making ATP (**chemiosmosis**). At the end the electrons, protons and oxygen form **water**. Each NADH gives about 3 ATP (older value) and each FADH$_2$ about 2.

**Total.** Classical: $2 + 2 + 34 = 38$ ATP per glucose (modern textbooks: about 30 to 32, since the transport of NADH into the mitochondrion and proton leakage cost some energy).

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the fate of pyruvate in anaerobic respiration? *[5 marks]* *(3, 12, 5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the absence (or shortage) of oxygen the link reaction, Krebs cycle and electron transport chain cannot work. Pyruvate stays in the **cytoplasm**, and is **reduced** by the NADH formed in glycolysis. This **regenerates NAD$^+$**, which is needed so that **glycolysis can continue** and make its small yield of **2 ATP** per glucose.

**1. In animal cells (e.g. muscle in vigorous exercise) and some bacteria: lactate fermentation**

$$\text{pyruvate} + NADH + H^+ \xrightarrow{\text{lactate dehydrogenase}} \text{lactate} + NAD^+$$

The lactate accumulates in the muscles (causing fatigue and cramps), is carried to the **liver** in the blood, and is later converted back to pyruvate and then to glucose or oxidised when oxygen is available again: this is the repayment of the **oxygen debt** (Cori cycle).

**2. In yeast and plant cells (e.g. waterlogged roots): alcoholic fermentation**

$$\text{pyruvate} \xrightarrow{\text{pyruvate decarboxylase}} \text{ethanal} + CO_2$$

$$\text{ethanal} + NADH + H^+ \xrightarrow{\text{alcohol dehydrogenase}} \text{ethanol} + NAD^+$$

Ethanol is toxic at a high concentration, and cannot be changed back to pyruvate; it is excreted or accumulates.

In both cases only about **2 ATP** per glucose are made, since the energy remains in the lactate or ethanol.
